Q: Microservices architecture: Should identity validation be centralized in a dedicated service or handled locally by each service? A:

I would do it all locally, using OpenID-Connect and the BFF pattern. Using BFF allows you to delete all the tokens on the backend when the user signs out or is revoked. So that solves most of your architectual authentication pains. Don't call the Identity provider on the hot path, that is also important if you want scale. the most important is the user experiene when users signs out. You can accept some "eventually consistency" for the tokens on the backend.

I did blog about these topics here:

  • Implementing BFF Pattern in ASP.NET Core for SPAs

  • Improving ASP.NET Core Security By Putting Your Cookies On A Diet
    (Benefits of storing the user tokens in the backend)

Q: JAVA bug returns 0 A:

did you ever think about machine properties in JAVA?

This is not a "machine property".

256*256*256*256 is an expression that is performed using 32 bit integer (int) arithmetic, and the computation overflows since the result is larger than 2^31 - 1.

However, if you wrote the statement as:

final long all=256L*256L*256L*256L;

or even

final long all=256L*256*256*256;

the expression would be evaluated using 64 bit integer arithmetic and you would get the result 4294967296.

There is nothing machine specific about this. This will happen for all JLS compliant Java implementations on all hardware platforms.

It is NOT a bug in Java. It is specified behavior.

Q: How do you use a c string (char array) in GCC with inline ARM assembly A:

You cannot pass a system register name as runtime string to inline assembly . The register encoding is baked into the instruction at compile time, not looked up by name at runtime.

The right approach is to use a preprocessor macro, not a function"

#define asm_mrs(sysreg, result) \
    __asm__ volatile("mrs %0, " #sysreg : "=r"(result))

Usage:

unsigned long val;
asm_mrs(CNTP_CTL_EL0, val);

The #sysreg stringification causes the preprocessor to paste CNTP_CTL_EL0 directly into the assembly template string before the compiler ever sees it, so the assembler gets the literal instruction mrs x0, CNTP_CTL_EL0 as intended

If you prefer function call syntax, you can wrap it:

#define asm_mrs(sysreg) ({ \
    unsigned long _r; \
    __asm__ volatile("mrs %0, " #sysreg : "=r"(_r)); \
    _r; \
})

unsigned long val = asm_mrs(CNTP_CTL_EL0);

The original attempt was passing the address of the string in a general purpose register as an "r" operand, the assembler would interpret that as a register operand, not a register name, which is why it doesn't work

Q: How does word boundary restriction deal with empty string at the end? A:

\b is a word boundary (so a begin or end of word).

\b matches between two characters, and does not consume any char.

It matches a changement from \w (word) to \W (not word) or from \W (not word) to \w (word), but also if it is at the begin or end of string. So it also matches between ^ and \w or between \w and $.

As soon as you use the g modifier, the regex engine will keep on searching for the pattern until it reaches the end of the string. The steps:

  1. The regex engine first matches "a" and consumes this character. If the string would have been "Zara", we would match "a" at the end of the string.

  2. The engine continues searching from this position (at the end of the string). There isn't any char left, but as a* means 0 or N times "a", it matches "", which effectively is followed by the end of a word. So this is why you get this second match, which is an empty string.

Proposition

As I mentionned in the comment below, if you don't want to match this ending empty string, you have to replace a* (0 or N times) by a+ (1 or N times).

Demonstration by testing

If your input string contains words not starting with "a", you'll even have several other empty string matches.

See it in action with these tests:

const inputs = [
  "a",
  "Sara",
  "Zara, tada!"
];

const patterns = [
  /a*\b/g, // 0 or N times "a", followed by a word boundary.
  /a+\b/g  // 1 or N times "a", followed by a word boundary.
];

for (const input of inputs) {
  for (const pattern of patterns) {
    console.log(`Execute ${pattern.toString()} on "${input}":\n`);
    const matches = [...input.matchAll(pattern)];
    for (const match of matches) {
      console.log(`\tIndex: ${match.index}\tValue: "${match[0]}"`);
    }
  }
}
